Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.

ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

8/10: A great immersive 'clicking sim' story game, with a couple of rough edges.

The good: I was completely engaged with the game from start to finish (binged it in 1 session). I felt that the difficulty, pacing and depth was just right for most of the game. The fact that the most minor of decisions are final and cannot be undone even though their consequences might not be realized until an hour or two later really kept me on my toes. While most of the game plays like a relaxing interactive story w/o difficulty there was just enough setpiece 'puzzles' (where a key decision required rereading every piece of information thoroughly and thinking hard) to create a good cycle of tension without feeling exhausting. And just when my brain was out of juice, the game ended. Beautiful

The bad: 1) the fact that the 'important information' to your investigation is hard-coded rather than free to deduce by yourself rears its ugly head occasionally. The developer, understandably, didn't account for every permutation that information might be read from. So, for example, when I'm asked to provide a portrait of a target and the game doesn't let me submit that one picture because the dev missed it it was a a little frustrating. It frustrates because, while minor, the immersion drops and the plot's rails become visible for just a second. 

*2 INVOLVES MINOR PLOT SPOILERS* TLDR: meh ending

[spoiler]2) The obligatory *twist ending* was not well executed. I imagine I'm not the first one to pick up on that given how glaringly it stands out from the quality of the rest of the game (can be read as a plus.). Arthur Conan Doyle's (Sherlock Holmes) rules of a good detective story require that the answer be obvious 'had you known X', ie there must be a underlying logic to it that the reader/player was only unable to uncover until the end due to not having all the pieces. The secret villain showed no indication that [hidden] was capable of performing the act even after everything was revealed, which makes the reveal feel like plain shock value. In fact I was absolutely caught off guard by the reveal when it was done through NPC dialog. 

To the devs: Objective fact reveals like "surprise he/she was actually secretly there" or "he/she is acting mysteriously" alone does not convince me that they are secretly the culprit. You gotta show motive, character, drives. Not what they did but why they did it.[/spoiler]

Overall, would absolutely say that the game nailed what it set out to do, i.e. letting you roleplay as a Big Brother spying and tearing through everyone's personal info on a quest to stop terrorism. And the moral of the story was made pretty well: guessing who someone is through their personal info alone without context is inaccurate. That the plot that came attached to that experience, and the human limitations of the dev, is a little underwhelming does not discount the fact that I was completely immersed into it. Which is a rare thing

A fascinating examination of a surveillance state in the modern age of connectedness and social networking. You play as an criminal investigator by trawling through personal conversations, private social media posts and transcribed phone calls looking for relevant information and, later, incriminating evidence. The onus is on the player to identify what is relevant; exposing ethical dilemmas around privacy, selective reporting of information and being intentionally mislead. 

Comparisons with novels like [b]1984[/b] are all bit invited by the game's title. While the novel had the benefit of originality, this game forces the player out of passive observation into an active role. While the game's events are fixed and the set of possible outcomes predetermined, the narrative the player weaves as they learn more about the actors is their own, leaving room for regret and introspection not possible through a novel. While we often construct narratives that we would always be "good people", games like [b]Orwell[/b] or [b]Papers Please[/b] challenge us to both be that person in difficult scenarios and to understand what "good" actually is.

A bit short with around seven hours of game play but worth it. However, there is a lot of reading and comprehension, which may put off those looking for something more cathartic than cerebral.
